action.description: One of 'publish', 'list', 'read', 'delete', 'open', 'pin', 'unpin', 'quickstart'. Omitting it means 'publish'. **Calls** in the description says what each one does and takes, except as noted here.

file_path.description: publish: the local page Claude publishes (.html, or .md only when a skill says so). For an Artifact created from an Artifact type, it is one of that Artifact's data files. With `asset: true`, it is the local file Claude uploads. A short, distinctive basename also serves as the title when nothing else gives one.

asset.description: publish with `url`: true uploads `file_path` (or each of `file_paths`) to that artifact's asset store instead of publishing it as the page — or, with `from_url` and `asset_ids` in place of `file_path`, copies those assets of another artifact into it server side (see **Calls**).

file_paths.description: publish with `asset: true` only: several local image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in place of `file_path`, up to 25 in one call, all into the artifact that `url` names; one approval covers the call, and the result lists each file's id and url, or why it was not uploaded. A CSV, Markdown, JSON or plain-text file, a symbolic or hard link, and a file outside the working directory each go in a call of their own with `file_path`.

from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes the published path of a `files` entry. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` is served at its path relative to `root`, unless a `files` map entry states its served path. Claude sends it with every such publish, set to the folder that holds the Artifact's files at their served paths.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

page_token.description: list only: the `next_page_token` a listing of the same scope gave, to list the artifacts after it.

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (writing people will keep editing or pass around as text, such as a memo, plan, spec, proposal or notes), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (a page to look at or use: an explainer, a diagram, anything interactive, a dashboard that shows data, a spreadsheet, anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

The user may see only the question dialog: tool results and text you wrote earlier in this turn may not be on their screen while it is open. Make each question stand on its own: if it depends on something you found, say so briefly, and name the items you are asking about in the question itself.

Preview feature:
Use the optional `preview` field on options when presenting concrete artifacts that users need to visually compare:
- ASCII mockups of UI layouts or components
- Code snippets showing different implementations
- Diagram variations
- Configuration examples

Preview content is rendered as markdown in a monospace box. Multi-line text with newlines is supported. When any option has a preview, the UI switches to a side-by-side layout with a vertical option list on the left and preview on the right. Do not use previews for simple preference questions where labels and descriptions suffice. Note: previews are only supported for single-select questions (not multiSelect).

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. You will be notified when it exits — do not poll its output file while waiting. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1

- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

1	# The RFQ Inbox — a four-day problem
2	
3	> Read *The situation*, then open the twenty-four dev emails, then come back for the rest. This
4	> document is short on purpose: most of what matters here is *your* judgment, not ours.
5	
6	## The situation
7	
8	You have just joined **Ridgeline Industrial Supply**, a distributor of pipe, fittings, flanges,
9	valves and bolting. Ridgeline's inside sales reps spend most of their day on one inbox:
10	customers asking for prices. On a good day that is a tidy list in the body of an email. Most
11	days it's a spreadsheet with "ALL PIPE SCH 40" in a merged cell above the rows that need it, a
12	phone photo of a list a foreman wrote on a clipboard, a scan of a scan, a reply that says
13	"make #3 twelve and kill #5" to an email from last week, a supplier's quote that looks exactly
14	like a customer's request, and a bounce notification with somebody's whole order attached.
15	
16	Every one of those has to become a clean list of what the customer wants — or a flag saying a
17	human needs to look — before anyone can quote it. A missed email is a customer who never
18	hears back. A line read wrong is a wrong quote.
19	
20	**Your job: build the thing that reads this inbox.** For every email, decide what kind of email
21	it is, and pull out exactly the items being asked for, each one self-contained — with the
22	schedule, material or rating that the customer wrote somewhere *other* than on that line.
23	
24	You will need a model to do it — several of these emails are photos and scans, and most of
25	the rest hide their meaning in headings, notes and threads. Calling a model is the easy part.
26	What we are assessing is **how you put it to work**: what it decides and what your code checks,
27	how you know it's right, what it costs, and what happens when it's wrong, slow, or down.
28	
29	## What you are given
30	
31	```
32	data/
33	  README.md            the contract: the command, the output format, how we grade — read it in full
34	  eml_to_json.py       optional helper: .eml → JSON + the attachment files
35	  check_format.py      validates your output's shape (it scores nothing)
36	  catalog.csv          what Ridgeline stocks — for the optional matcher
37	  dev/
38	    emails/*.eml       24 inbox emails
39	    answer_key.json    what a careful rep made of each one — your ground truth
40	```
41	
42	There is also a **held-out inbox** of ~40 emails from the same company — the same kinds of
43	customers, documents and surprises, none of the same strings, and a few situations dev doesn't
44	show you. We run your submission against it. Work that passes dev by fitting it will not
45	survive that; work built from understanding *why* dev is hard will. All data is synthetic.
46	
47	## What to build
48	
49	One command, exactly as `data/README.md` defines it:
50	
51	```
52	parse --emails <dir> --out parsed.json
53	```
54	
55	Per email: a **classification** (seven kinds), the **line items** (verbatim text,
56	self-contained description, quantity, unit, where it came from), and a **needs-review** flag
57	for when you can't — or shouldn't — answer alone.
58	
59	**Build it like it will run on the real inbox tomorrow.** Four properties are required, and we
60	test each of them:
61	
62	1. **Replayable.** On the dev inbox it runs with **no API key** — record or cache model
63	   responses and commit them.
64	2. **Idempotent and cheap to re-run.** Running it twice on the same inbox makes no new model
65	   calls the second time.
66	3. **One bad email never takes down the run.** Some attachments are broken on purpose; some
67	   things are unreadable for anyone. Those come back flagged, and the run carries on.
68	4. **You know what it cost.** Tell us the model calls, tokens and dollars per email on dev.
69	
70	## Optional — if you have time left
71	
72	Never required, never penalised when skipped. If you build the matcher we run its numbers too,
73	but both parts are weighed in the interview, not in your score. Both are good places to show
74	judgment the core can't.
75	
76	- **The matcher, designed (and built if you like).** Each extracted line eventually has to
77	  become a catalog part — or a decision that Ridgeline doesn't stock it. The catalog does not
78	  carry everything customers ask for, and the closest part is often one attribute off (right
79	  size, wrong schedule). Write down how you'd decide: what you normalise, which attributes
80	  must agree, how you find candidates, when the answer is **not in catalog** and when it is
81	  "ask the customer", where a model helps and what it must never decide on its own, and how
82	  you'd measure it. A page in `DECISIONS.md` or a separate `MATCHER.md`. If you build it, add
83	  the optional `sku` / `match` fields `data/README.md` defines — `dev/answer_key.json` has
84	  the answers for dev.
85	- **A small web app** that walks one email through your system: the email and its
86	  attachments, the lines you extracted and where each came from, and — if you built the
87	  matcher — each line's catalog match or not-in-catalog decision, which a rep can accept or
88	  overturn. Clarity is worth something; polish is worth nothing.
89	
90	## What to hand in
91	
92	A git repository — zipped, on Google Drive, or on GitHub (see *Logistics*) — containing:
93	
94	1. **The code**, with `RUNNING.md`: one setup step from a fresh clone or unzip to a working
95	   `parse`, the model(s) you use, and what a run costs.
96	2. **`parsed.json` for dev**, regenerated by your command.
97	3. **`DECISIONS.md`** — at most two pages. These four headed sections are **required**:
98	   - *Something in the data that surprised you* — one paragraph.
99	   - *Something in this brief or the README you disagree with, and what you did about it.*
100	     We mean it; the README is not gospel.
101	   - *Your predicted held-out numbers, and the two kinds of email you expect to get wrong.*
102	     We will compare.
103	   - *How this runs for real.* Three thousand emails a day arrive by webhook. The model
104	     provider is down for two hours. A customer sends a 300-page PDF. The same email is
105	     delivered twice. What happens in your design — and which of those did you actually
106	     build?
107	
108	   Plus whatever else belongs in a design memo: where the model decides and where code
109	   decides, how you measured it, what you rejected, what you know is broken, what's next.
110	   Be specific to *this* data.
111	4. **`AI_USAGE.md`** — at most one page, how you used AI coding agents (Claude Code, Codex,
112	   Cursor, Copilot — whatever you use for real work), with these headings:
113	   - *Setup* — which tools and models; instruction files, subagents, skills, MCP servers.
114	   - *How you worked* — one paragraph: how you split the work, planned, tested and reviewed.
115	   - *Three moments* — the agent was wrong and how you caught it; you overruled it and why;
116	     it saved you real time. Each points at a commit hash **and** the session it happened in.
117	5. **`ai-sessions/`** — the raw session logs of your coding agents for this project, unedited
118	   except for redacted secrets: Claude Code — the `.jsonl` files under
119	   `~/.claude/projects/<your-project-folder>/` (or `/export` from each session); Codex CLI —
120	   `~/.codex/sessions/`; Cursor, Copilot and others — export or copy each chat. Include every
121	   instruction you gave the agents (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, rules files, subagent or skill
122	   definitions, saved prompts). We read **how you directed the tools** — what you asked for,
123	   what you checked, what you threw away — not how much of the code you typed. If your tool
124	   can't export, say so in `AI_USAGE.md` and bring the history to the interview. **Before you
125	   send:** search the folder for `sk-` and redact any key (agents often echo `.env` files into
126	   tool output), and include only this project's instruction files — nothing personal or
127	   belonging to an employer.
128	6. **A screen recording, five minutes or less** — one email end to end through your system,
129	   the two decisions you'd defend first, and one moment from your agent sessions where you
130	   changed the agent's course. Production value is worth nothing. Link it in
131	   `RUNNING.md` or commit it (keep the repo under 50 MB).
132	7. **Commit history as it happened** — a zip must include the `.git` folder; a GitHub repo
133	   carries it already. Don't squash or tidy it for us.
134	
135	## Rules
136	
137	- **Time.** The package arrives **Thursday 12 November**; submission is due **Sunday
138	  15 November, 23:59 CST** — and the moment you're done is the moment to send it. We expect **8–12 hours of work** and grade for that budget. Past 16
139	  hours: stop and write. Tell us in `DECISIONS.md` roughly how long you spent. If this window
140	  doesn't work for you, say so and we'll move it.
141	- **Stack.** Anything that runs for us: we run submissions on **Windows — natively, in Docker,
142	  or under WSL** — with Python 3.11+, Node 20 and Docker available. If your stack assumes
143	  Linux, ship a Dockerfile; either way, say what we need in `RUNNING.md`.
144	- **Model access.** The email this package came with includes an **OpenAI API key with a USD
145	  20 cap**. It is for your `parse` command — run your coding agents on your own accounts. Read
146	  it from `OPENAI_API_KEY` and name the model(s) in `RUNNING.md`. We run the held-out inbox
147	  **with an OpenAI key only**, so your default path must use OpenAI; another provider is
148	  welcome as an option you switch on, at your own cost. If the key is missing or a call fails,
149	  your system degrades the way you designed it to — it never crashes.
150	- **Don't fit the dev set.** The held-out inbox has the same *kinds* of surprises, not the same
151	  strings.
152	- **No outbound side effects.** Nothing in your submission sends email or calls anything except
153	  the model provider.
154	
155	## How we read it
156	
157	We run `parse` on the held-out inbox **before we read a word you wrote** — once with our key,
158	then again with the key removed (property 2 says that second run should match, from your
159	cache). Then `DECISIONS.md`, the recording, the code, the commits, `AI_USAGE.md` and your
160	agent sessions. Then a 60-minute conversation: you show us the two emails you find most
161	interesting, predict what your system will do with an email you've never seen before we run
162	it, defend two decisions, and change something live — with whatever tools you normally use.
163	We watch where you look first and what test you name.
164	
165	Two pages that name three real properties of this data beat a feature you rushed.
166	
167	## Logistics
168	
169	- **Submit:** reply to the email this package came with, carrying **one** of: a GitHub
170	  repository link (if it's private, ask in your reply and we'll tell you who to add); a Google
171	  Drive link to the zip (project folder including `.git`, fixtures committed); or the zip
172	  attached — but mail servers often reject zips containing scripts and cap attachments around
173	  25 MB, so prefer a link. Code and recording both.
174	- **Your code stays yours.** We use it only to evaluate you and delete it when the process ends.
175	- **Questions:** reply on the same email thread. We answer **08:00–17:00 CST every day,
176	  weekend included**, usually within a few hours. We answer questions about the data and the
177	  format; we won't tell you what to build.

valves and bolting. Ridgeline's inside sales reps spend most of their day on one inbox:
customers asking for prices. On a good day that is a tidy list in the body of an email. Most
days it's a spreadsheet with "ALL PIPE SCH 40" in a merged cell above the rows that need it, a
phone photo of a list a foreman wrote on a clipboard, a scan of a scan, a reply that says
"make #3 twelve and kill #5" to an email from last week, a supplier's quote that looks exactly
like a customer's request, and a bounce notification with somebody's whole order attached.

Every one of those has to become a clean list of what the customer wants — or a flag saying a
human needs to look — before anyone can quote it. A missed email is a customer who never
hears back. A line read wrong is a wrong quote.

**Your job: build the thing that reads this inbox.** For every email, decide what kind of email
it is, and pull out exactly the items being asked for, each one self-contained — with the
schedule, material or rating that the customer wrote somewhere *other* than on that line.

You will need a model to do it — several of these emails are photos and scans, and most of
the rest hide their meaning in headings, notes and threads. Calling a model is the easy part.
What we are assessing is **how you put it to work**: what it decides and what your code checks,
how you know it's right, what it costs, and what happens when it's wrong, slow, or down.

## What you are given

```
data/
  README.md            the contract: the command, the output format, how we grade — read it in full
  eml_to_json.py       optional helper: .eml → JSON + the attachment files
  check_format.py      validates your output's shape (it scores nothing)
  catalog.csv          what Ridgeline stocks — for the optional matcher
  dev/
    emails/*.eml       24 inbox emails
    answer_key.json    what a careful rep made of each one — your ground truth
```

There is also a **held-out inbox** of ~40 emails from the same company — the same kinds of
customers, documents and surprises, none of the same strings, and a few situations dev doesn't
show you. We run your submission against it. Work that passes dev by fitting it will not
survive that; work built from understanding *why* dev is hard will. All data is synthetic.

## What to build

One command, exactly as `data/README.md` defines it:

```
parse --emails <dir> --out parsed.json
```

Per email: a **classification** (seven kinds), the **line items** (verbatim text,
self-contained description, quantity, unit, where it came from), and a **needs-review** flag
for when you can't — or shouldn't — answer alone.

**Build it like it will run on the real inbox tomorrow.** Four properties are required, and we
test each of them:

1. **Replayable.** On the dev inbox it runs with **no API key** — record or cache model
   responses and commit them.
2. **Idempotent and cheap to re-run.** Running it twice on the same inbox makes no new model
   calls the second time.
3. **One bad email never takes down the run.** Some attachments are broken on purpose; some
   things are unreadable for anyone. Those come back flagged, and the run carries on.
4. **You know what it cost.** Tell us the model calls, tokens and dollars per email on dev.

## Optional — if you have time left

Never required, never penalised when skipped. If you build the matcher we run its numbers too,
but both parts are weighed in the interview, not in your score. Both are good places to show
judgment the core can't.

- **The matcher, designed (and built if you like).** Each extracted line eventually has to
  become a catalog part — or a decision that Ridgeline doesn't stock it. The catalog does not
  carry everything customers ask for, and the closest part is often one attribute off (right
  size, wrong schedule). Write down how you'd decide: what you normalise, which attributes
  must agree, how you find candidates, when the answer is **not in catalog** and when it is
  "ask the customer", where a model helps and what it must never decide on its own, and how
  you'd measure it. A page in `DECISIONS.md` or a separate `MATCHER.md`. If you build it, add
  the optional `sku` / `match` fields `data/README.md` defines — `dev/answer_key.json` has
  the answers for dev.
- **A small web app** that walks one email through your system: the email and its
  attachments, the lines you extracted and where each came from, and — if you built the
  matcher — each line's catalog match or not-in-catalog decision, which a rep can accept or
  overturn. Clarity is worth something; polish is worth nothing.

## What to hand in

A git repository — zipped, on Google Drive, or on GitHub (see *Logistics*) — containing:

1. **The code**, with `RUNNING.md`: one setup step from a fresh clone or unzip to a working
   `parse`, the model(s) you use, and what a run costs.
2. **`parsed.json` for dev**, regenerated by your command.
3. **`DECISIONS.md`** — at most two pages. These four headed sections are **required**:
   - *Something in the data that surprised you* — one paragraph.
   - *Something in this brief or the README you disagree with, and what you did about it.*
     We mean it; the README is not gospel.
   - *Your predicted held-out numbers, and the two kinds of email you expect to get wrong.*
     We will compare.
   - *How this runs for real.* Three thousand emails a day arrive by webhook. The model
     provider is down for two hours. A customer sends a 300-page PDF. The same email is
     delivered twice. What happens in your design — and which of those did you actually
     build?

   Plus whatever else belongs in a design memo: where the model decides and where code
   decides, how you measured it, what you rejected, what you know is broken, what's next.
   Be specific to *this* data.
4. **`AI_USAGE.md`** — at most one page, how you used AI coding agents (Claude Code, Codex,
   Cursor, Copilot — whatever you use for real work), with these headings:
   - *Setup* — which tools and models; instruction files, subagents, skills, MCP servers.
   - *How you worked* — one paragraph: how you split the work, planned, tested and reviewed.
   - *Three moments* — the agent was wrong and how you caught it; you overruled it and why;
     it saved you real time. Each points at a commit hash **and** the session it happened in.
5. **`ai-sessions/`** — the raw session logs of your coding agents for this project, unedited
   except for redacted secrets: Claude Code — the `.jsonl` files under
   `~/.claude/projects/<your-project-folder>/` (or `/export` from each session); Codex CLI —
   `~/.codex/sessions/`; Cursor, Copilot and others — export or copy each chat. Include every
   instruction you gave the agents (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, rules files, subagent or skill
   definitions, saved prompts). We read **how you directed the tools** — what you asked for,
   what you checked, what you threw away — not how much of the code you typed. If your tool
   can't export, say so in `AI_USAGE.md` and bring the history to the interview. **Before you
   send:** search the folder for `sk-` and redact any key (agents often echo `.env` files into
   tool output), and include only this project's instruction files — nothing personal or
   belonging to an employer.
6. **A screen recording, five minutes or less** — one email end to end through your system,
   the two decisions you'd defend first, and one moment from your agent sessions where you
   changed the agent's course. Production value is worth nothing. Link it in
   `RUNNING.md` or commit it (keep the repo under 50 MB).
7. **Commit history as it happened** — a zip must include the `.git` folder; a GitHub repo
   carries it already. Don't squash or tidy it for us.

## Rules

- **Time.** The package arrives **Thursday 12 November**; submission is due **Sunday
  15 November, 23:59 CST** — and the moment you're done is the moment to send it. We expect **8–12 hours of work** and grade for that budget. Past 16
  hours: stop and write. Tell us in `DECISIONS.md` roughly how long you spent. If this window
  doesn't work for you, say so and we'll move it.
- **Stack.** Anything that runs for us: we run submissions on **Windows — natively, in Docker,
  or under WSL** — with Python 3.11+, Node 20 and Docker available. If your stack assumes
  Linux, ship a Dockerfile; either way, say what we need in `RUNNING.md`.
- **Model access.** The email this package came with includes an **OpenAI API key with a USD
  20 cap**. It is for your `parse` command — run your coding agents on your own accounts. Read
  it from `OPENAI_API_KEY` and name the model(s) in `RUNNING.md`. We run the held-out inbox
  **with an OpenAI key only**, so your default path must use OpenAI; another provider is
  welcome as an option you switch on, at your own cost. If the key is missing or a call fails,
  your system degrades the way you designed it to — it never crashes.
- **Don't fit the dev set.** The held-out inbox has the same *kinds* of surprises, not the same
  strings.
- **No outbound side effects.** Nothing in your submission sends email or calls anything except
  the model provider.

## How we read it

We run `parse` on the held-out inbox **before we read a word you wrote** — once with our key,
then again with the key removed (property 2 says that second run should match, from your
cache). Then `DECISIONS.md`, the recording, the code, the commits, `AI_USAGE.md` and your
agent sessions. Then a 60-minute conversation: you show us the two emails you find most
interesting, predict what your system will do with an email you've never seen before we run
it, defend two decisions, and change something live — with whatever tools you normally use.
We watch where you look first and what test you name.

Two pages that name three real properties of this data beat a feature you rushed.

## Logistics

- **Submit:** reply to the email this package came with, carrying **one** of: a GitHub
  repository link (if it's private, ask in your reply and we'll tell you who to add); a Google
  Drive link to the zip (project folder including `.git`, fixtures committed); or the zip
  attached — but mail servers often reject zips containing scripts and cap attachments around
  25 MB, so prefer a link. Code and recording both.
- **Your code stays yours.** We use it only to evaluate you and delete it when the process ends.
- **Questions:** reply on the same email thread. We answer **08:00–17:00 CST every day,
  weekend included**, usually within a few hours. We answer questions about the data and the
  format; we won't tell you what to build.

1	# The RFQ Inbox — a four-day problem
2	
3	> Read *The situation*, then open the twenty-four dev emails, then come back for the rest. This
4	> document is short on purpose: most of what matters here is *your* judgment, not ours.
5	
6	## The situation
7	
8	You have just joined **Ridgeline Industrial Supply**, a distributor of pipe, fittings, flanges,
9	valves and bolting. Ridgeline's inside sales reps spend most of their day on one inbox:
10	customers asking for prices. On a good day that is a tidy list in the body of an email. Most
11	days it's a spreadsheet with "ALL PIPE SCH 40" in a merged cell above the rows that need it, a
12	phone photo of a list a foreman wrote on a clipboard, a scan of a scan, a reply that says
13	"make #3 twelve and kill #5" to an email from last week, a supplier's quote that looks exactly
14	like a customer's request, and a bounce notification with somebody's whole order attached.
15	
16	Every one of those has to become a clean list of what the customer wants — or a flag saying a
17	human needs to look — before anyone can quote it. A missed email is a customer who never
18	hears back. A line read wrong is a wrong quote.
19	
20	**Your job: build the thing that reads this inbox.** For every email, decide what kind of email
21	it is, and pull out exactly the items being asked for, each one self-contained — with the
22	schedule, material or rating that the customer wrote somewhere *other* than on that line.
23	
24	You will need a model to do it — several of these emails are photos and scans, and most of
25	the rest hide their meaning in headings, notes and threads. Calling a model is the easy part.
26	What we are assessing is **how you put it to work**: what it decides and what your code checks,
27	how you know it's right, what it costs, and what happens when it's wrong, slow, or down.
28	
29	## What you are given
30	
31	```
32	data/
33	  README.md            the contract: the command, the output format, how we grade — read it in full
34	  eml_to_json.py       optional helper: .eml → JSON + the attachment files
35	  check_format.py      validates your output's shape (it scores nothing)
36	  catalog.csv          what Ridgeline stocks — for the optional matcher
37	  dev/
38	    emails/*.eml       24 inbox emails
39	    answer_key.json    what a careful rep made of each one — your ground truth
40	```
41	
42	There is also a **held-out inbox** of ~40 emails from the same company — the same kinds of
43	customers, documents and surprises, none of the same strings, and a few situations dev doesn't
44	show you. We run your submission against it. Work that passes dev by fitting it will not
45	survive that; work built from understanding *why* dev is hard will. All data is synthetic.
46	
47	## What to build
48	
49	One command, exactly as `data/README.md` defines it:
50	
51	```
52	parse --emails <dir> --out parsed.json
53	```
54	
55	Per email: a **classification** (seven kinds), the **line items** (verbatim text,
56	self-contained description, quantity, unit, where it came from), and a **needs-review** flag
57	for when you can't — or shouldn't — answer alone.
58	
59	**Build it like it will run on the real inbox tomorrow.** Four properties are required, and we
60	test each of them:
61	
62	1. **Replayable.** On the dev inbox it runs with **no API key** — record or cache model
63	   responses and commit them.
64	2. **Idempotent and cheap to re-run.** Running it twice on the same inbox makes no new model
65	   calls the second time.
66	3. **One bad email never takes down the run.** Some attachments are broken on purpose; some
67	   things are unreadable for anyone. Those come back flagged, and the run carries on.
68	4. **You know what it cost.** Tell us the model calls, tokens and dollars per email on dev.
69	
70	## Optional — if you have time left
71	
72	Never required, never penalised when skipped. If you build the matcher we run its numbers too,
73	but both parts are weighed in the interview, not in your score. Both are good places to show
74	judgment the core can't.
75	
76	- **The matcher, designed (and built if you like).** Each extracted line eventually has to
77	  become a catalog part — or a decision that Ridgeline doesn't stock it. The catalog does not
78	  carry everything customers ask for, and the closest part is often one attribute off (right
79	  size, wrong schedule). Write down how you'd decide: what you normalise, which attributes
80	  must agree, how you find candidates, when the answer is **not in catalog** and when it is
81	  "ask the customer", where a model helps and what it must never decide on its own, and how
82	  you'd measure it. A page in `DECISIONS.md` or a separate `MATCHER.md`. If you build it, add
83	  the optional `sku` / `match` fields `data/README.md` defines — `dev/answer_key.json` has
84	  the answers for dev.
85	- **A small web app** that walks one email through your system: the email and its
86	  attachments, the lines you extracted and where each came from, and — if you built the
87	  matcher — each line's catalog match or not-in-catalog decision, which a rep can accept or
88	  overturn. Clarity is worth something; polish is worth nothing.
89	
90	## What to hand in
91	
92	A git repository — zipped, on Google Drive, or on GitHub (see *Logistics*) — containing:
93	
94	1. **The code**, with `RUNNING.md`: one setup step from a fresh clone or unzip to a working
95	   `parse`, the model(s) you use, and what a run costs.
96	2. **`parsed.json` for dev**, regenerated by your command.
97	3. **`DECISIONS.md`** — at most two pages. These four headed sections are **required**:
98	   - *Something in the data that surprised you* — one paragraph.
99	   - *Something in this brief or the README you disagree with, and what you did about it.*
100	     We mean it; the README is not gospel.
101	   - *Your predicted held-out numbers, and the two kinds of email you expect to get wrong.*
102	     We will compare.
103	   - *How this runs for real.* Three thousand emails a day arrive by webhook. The model
104	     provider is down for two hours. A customer sends a 300-page PDF. The same email is
105	     delivered twice. What happens in your design — and which of those did you actually
106	     build?
107	
108	   Plus whatever else belongs in a design memo: where the model decides and where code
109	   decides, how you measured it, what you rejected, what you know is broken, what's next.
110	   Be specific to *this* data.
111	4. **`AI_USAGE.md`** — at most one page, how you used AI coding agents (Claude Code, Codex,
112	   Cursor, Copilot — whatever you use for real work), with these headings:
113	   - *Setup* — which tools and models; instruction files, subagents, skills, MCP servers.
114	   - *How you worked* — one paragraph: how you split the work, planned, tested and reviewed.
115	   - *Three moments* — the agent was wrong and how you caught it; you overruled it and why;
116	     it saved you real time. Each points at a commit hash **and** the session it happened in.
117	5. **`ai-sessions/`** — the raw session logs of your coding agents for this project, unedited
118	   except for redacted secrets: Claude Code — the `.jsonl` files under
119	   `~/.claude/projects/<your-project-folder>/` (or `/export` from each session); Codex CLI —
120	   `~/.codex/sessions/`; Cursor, Copilot and others — export or copy each chat. Include every
121	   instruction you gave the agents (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, rules files, subagent or skill
122	   definitions, saved prompts). We read **how you directed the tools** — what you asked for,
123	   what you checked, what you threw away — not how much of the code you typed. If your tool
124	   can't export, say so in `AI_USAGE.md` and bring the history to the interview. **Before you
125	   send:** search the folder for `sk-` and redact any key (agents often echo `.env` files into
126	   tool output), and include only this project's instruction files — nothing personal or
127	   belonging to an employer.
128	6. **A screen recording, five minutes or less** — one email end to end through your system,
129	   the two decisions you'd defend first, and one moment from your agent sessions where you
130	   changed the agent's course. Production value is worth nothing. Link it in
131	   `RUNNING.md` or commit it (keep the repo under 50 MB).
132	7. **Commit history as it happened** — a zip must include the `.git` folder; a GitHub repo
133	   carries it already. Don't squash or tidy it for us.
134	
135	## Rules
136	
137	- **Time.** The package arrives **Thursday 12 November**; submission is due **Sunday
138	  15 November, 23:59 CST** — and the moment you're done is the moment to send it. We expect **8–12 hours of work** and grade for that budget. Past 16
139	  hours: stop and write. Tell us in `DECISIONS.md` roughly how long you spent. If this window
140	  doesn't work for you, say so and we'll move it.
141	- **Stack.** Anything that runs for us: we run submissions on **Windows — natively, in Docker,
142	  or under WSL** — with Python 3.11+, Node 20 and Docker available. If your stack assumes
143	  Linux, ship a Dockerfile; either way, say what we need in `RUNNING.md`.
144	- **Model access.** The email this package came with includes an **OpenAI API key with a USD
145	  20 cap**. It is for your `parse` command — run your coding agents on your own accounts. Read
146	  it from `OPENAI_API_KEY` and name the model(s) in `RUNNING.md`. We run the held-out inbox
147	  **with an OpenAI key only**, so your default path must use OpenAI; another provider is
148	  welcome as an option you switch on, at your own cost. If the key is missing or a call fails,
149	  your system degrades the way you designed it to — it never crashes.
150	- **Don't fit the dev set.** The held-out inbox has the same *kinds* of surprises, not the same
151	  strings.
152	- **No outbound side effects.** Nothing in your submission sends email or calls anything except
153	  the model provider.
154	
155	## How we read it
156	
157	We run `parse` on the held-out inbox **before we read a word you wrote** — once with our key,
158	then again with the key removed (property 2 says that second run should match, from your
159	cache). Then `DECISIONS.md`, the recording, the code, the commits, `AI_USAGE.md` and your
160	agent sessions. Then a 60-minute conversation: you show us the two emails you find most
161	interesting, predict what your system will do with an email you've never seen before we run
162	it, defend two decisions, and change something live — with whatever tools you normally use.
163	We watch where you look first and what test you name.
164	
165	Two pages that name three real properties of this data beat a feature you rushed.
166	
167	## Logistics
168	
169	- **Submit:** reply to the email this package came with, carrying **one** of: a GitHub
170	  repository link (if it's private, ask in your reply and we'll tell you who to add); a Google
171	  Drive link to the zip (project folder including `.git`, fixtures committed); or the zip
172	  attached — but mail servers often reject zips containing scripts and cap attachments around
173	  25 MB, so prefer a link. Code and recording both.
174	- **Your code stays yours.** We use it only to evaluate you and delete it when the process ends.
175	- **Questions:** reply on the same email thread. We answer **08:00–17:00 CST every day,
176	  weekend included**, usually within a few hours. We answer questions about the data and the
177	  format; we won't tell you what to build.

1	# data/ — the files, the contract, the grading
2	
3	```
4	dev/emails/*.eml       the inbox: 24 RFC-822 emails (E001.eml …) — plain text, HTML, Excel,
5	                       CSV, Word, text PDFs, scanned PDFs, phone photos, pasted screenshots, threads
6	dev/answer_key.json    what a careful inside sales rep (ISR) made of each email — your ground truth
7	check_format.py        validates the shape of your output (it scores nothing)
8	catalog.csv            what Ridgeline stocks — used only by the OPTIONAL matcher (see the end)
9	eml_to_json.py         optional: .eml → JSON + the attachment files. Use it, port it, or ignore it —
10	                       unpacking MIME is not what we grade; reading what is inside the attachments is.
11	```
12	
13	A **held-out inbox** from the same company — same kinds of customers, documents and surprises,
14	none of the same strings — is not shipped; your submission is run against it.
15	
16	## The command (this is how we run you, so the shape is mandatory)
17	
18	```
19	<your command> parse --emails <dir> --out parsed.json
20	```
21	
22	It reads every `.eml` in `<dir>` and writes one JSON file. Check it with
23	`python check_format.py parsed.json --emails <dir>` (exit 0 = shape ok).
24	
25	## parsed.json
26	
27	One object keyed by the `.eml` filename stem. **Every email in the directory must appear.**
28	
29	```json
30	{
31	  "E003": {
32	    "classification": "rfq",
33	    "revises": null,
34	    "duplicate_of": null,
35	    "needs_review": false,
36	    "review_reason": null,
37	    "line_items": [
38	      {
39	        "raw": "2\" x 21' - 12 lengths",
40	        "description": "2\" pipe, SCH 40 A53B ERW, threaded & coupled, 21' lengths",
41	        "qty": 12,
42	        "uom": "EA",
43	        "source": "body"
44	      }
45	    ]
46	  }
47	}
48	```
49	
50	### classification — exactly one per email
51	
52	| value | the **current** message … | line_items |
53	|---|---|---|
54	| `rfq` | asks us to price or check availability of items | the items |
55	| `rfq_revision` | changes a request made earlier in the same thread (quantities, additions, removals) | the **complete** order as now intended; `revises` = the earlier email's id if it is in the inbox, else null |
56	| `purchase_order` | commits to buy — a PO, "please process", "go ahead with items 1–3" | the items ordered |
57	| `vendor_quote` | is a supplier quoting or answering **us** | `[]` |
58	| `status_inquiry` | asks about an existing quote or order (update? ETA? tracking?) | `[]` |
59	| `auto_reply` | is machine-generated: out-of-office, bounce, receipt | `[]` |
60	| `other` | anything else: marketing, invoices and remittances, job applications, internal chatter, "we went with someone else" | `[]` |
61	
62	Classify what the current message *does* — not the subject line, not the quoted history.
63	
64	### line_items — one per thing the customer is asking for
65	
66	- **What counts.** Items in the current message, its attachments and pasted pictures, and —
67	  when one of our own reps forwards a customer's email — in the forwarded content. Not items
68	  in quoted earlier messages (they were handled when they arrived), not headings, notes,
69	  totals, prices, signatures, crossed-out lines, or old revisions of a document.
70	- **`raw`** — the line's text as it appears where you found it (a table row's cells on one
71	  line; for a picture or scan, your reading of it). We pair your lines with ours on these
72	  tokens, so keep it close to the source.
73	- **`description`** — the item **self-contained**, as an ISR would type it into a quote
74	  without re-reading the email: the line's own words plus every heading, note, column
75	  header, sheet name, form field, subject line or earlier line that applies to it — and
76	  nothing that doesn't apply to it. Never invent a spec the email doesn't give.
77	- **`qty` / `uom`** — as the customer stated it, not converted. A number spelled out is a
78	  number; a vague amount ("a couple", "enough for the job") is `null`. A size, schedule,
79	  length, rating, part number or price is never a quantity. `uom` is one of `EA FT M IN BX
80	  PK PR DZ RL LB SET GAL BAG CS`, or `null` when no unit is stated (we read `null` as `EA`).
81	- **`source`** — `"body"`, or the filename of the attachment / pasted image the line came from.
82	
83	### Threads, duplicates, forwards
84	
85	- A reply that changes an earlier request → `rfq_revision` with the **complete** order as the
86	  customer now intends it; the earlier email keeps its own lines as they were on arrival.
87	- The same request sent twice → **the email with the later `Date:` is the duplicate**: same
88	  classification as the original, `duplicate_of` = the original's id, `line_items: []`.
89	- Anything **from** `@ridgeline-supply.example` is one of our own reps, usually forwarding a
90	  customer's email; classify it as the customer's email, and read the rep's own note too.
91	
92	### needs_review — "a human has to look at this before anyone quotes it"
93	
94	`true` when the email asks for something you cannot fully read or resolve: the attachment it
95	points at is missing or can't be opened, or the items themselves are only identified by
96	something that isn't in the email ("same as our last order, but double it"). Put the reason in `review_reason` (required when `true`) and still
97	return whatever lines you *could* read. Only for `rfq`, `rfq_revision` and `purchase_order`.
98	
99	## Optional: matching to the catalog
100	
101	If you build the optional matcher, add three fields to each line item:
102	
103	```json
104	{"raw": "...", "description": "...", "qty": 12, "uom": "EA", "source": "body",
105	 "sku": "RL-12345", "match": "matched", "match_reason": "2\" 150# RF weld neck A105: one part fits"}
106	```
107	
108	- `match` is one of `matched` (exactly one catalog part is what the customer asked for —
109	  `sku` is it), `not_in_catalog` (we don't stock it — `sku: null`), or `ambiguous` (more than
110	  one stocked part fits what the customer wrote and they'd have to choose — `sku: null`,
111	  optional `candidates: [skus]`).
112	- `match_reason` — one short line a rep can check.
113	- **Not in catalog is a decision, not a failure.** Ridgeline doesn't stock everything
114	  customers ask for, and the nearest catalog part is often one attribute away — right size and
115	  type, wrong schedule, rating or material. Quoting that part is a wrong quote.
116	- `catalog.csv` columns: `sku, description, category, product, size, spec` (schedule or
117	  pressure class)`, material, ends, extra, uom`. Descriptions are abbreviated the way an ERP
118	  prints them.
119	
120	## World facts
121	
122	- Ridgeline Industrial Supply sells pipe, fittings, flanges, valves, gaskets, bolting and
123	  related industrial supplies. The RFQ inbox is `rfq@ridgeline-supply.example`.
124	- Our quotes are numbered `Q-26-…`. Customers' RFQ and PO numbers are theirs.
125	- A supplier answering *our* request for pricing is a `vendor_quote`, however much it looks
126	  like a list of items.
127	
128	## What we grade
129	
130	Your `parse` command on the held-out inbox, against our key, **before we read anything you wrote**.
131	
132	**Headline numbers** — the expensive failures, in this order:
133	1. **Silent losses** — an email that needed someone to act (it has items, or needs review)
134	   came back with no lines and no review flag. That customer never hears back.
135	2. **Hallucinated lines** — lines that aren't requests: quoted history, headings, prices,
136	   signatures, crossed-out or superseded rows.
137	3. **Lost and phantom requests** — a request classified as something else (lost), or a
138	   vendor quote / bounce / newsletter classified as a request (phantom).
139	
140	Then: classification accuracy, line recall and precision, and on paired lines — `qty`,
141	`uom`, `source`, and **context carried** (does the `description` mention what the key's
142	`must_mention` lists, and none of its `must_not_mention`?). Plus `revises` / `duplicate_of`
143	links and `needs_review` precision/recall.
144	
145	**Optional matcher**, if present: confident wrong matches (you named a part; the answer was a
146	different part, *not in catalog*, or *ambiguous*), not-in-catalog recall, and match accuracy.
147	
148	**`answer_key.json` fields beyond the schema:** `id` (`<email>-<n>`); `qty_tol` (relative
149	tolerance on qty: `0` exact, `null` = unscored); `must_mention` (phrases the description must
150	contain; `"a|b"` = either; case, spaces and punctuation ignored, and common spellings of the
151	same spec count as equal — Sch/Schedule, 150#/150 lb/Class 150, BW/butt weld, threaded/NPT,
152	SMLS/seamless, galv/galvanized, and the catalog's abbreviations ELL, VLV, FLG, GSKT, SPW, MI,
153	CS, FP, RED, CPLG); `must_not_mention` (phrases
154	it must not contain — a default that this line overrides, or a note that belongs to another
155	section); `sku` / `match` / `candidates` (the catalog answer for the optional matcher).

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Optional helper: .eml -> JSON + attachment files.  Use it, port it, or ignore it.  Stdlib only.

    python eml_to_json.py dev/emails/E001.eml                      # one email -> stdout
    python eml_to_json.py dev/emails --out inbox.json --files att  # all emails; attachments saved

Shape: {id, headers{from,to,cc,date,subject,message_id,in_reply_to,references},
        text, html, attachments:[{filename, mime, size, inline, content_id, path}]}
`path` is set only with --files (bytes written to <files>/<id>/<filename>).  A forwarded or
bounced message attached as message/rfc822 is saved as a .eml file.  Reading what is INSIDE an
attachment (Excel, PDF, scans, photos ...) is up to you.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import re
import sys
from email import policy
from email.parser import BytesParser
from pathlib import Path

HEADERS = ("from", "to", "cc", "date", "subject", "message-id", "in-reply-to", "references")


def _text(part) -> str:
    try:
        return part.get_content()
    except Exception:  # unknown charset / bad transfer encoding
        return (part.get_payload(decode=True) or b"").decode("utf-8", "replace")


def _safe(name: str) -> str:
    return re.sub(r"[^\w.\- ]+", "_", name).strip() or "unnamed"


def eml_to_json(path: Path, files: Path | None = None) -> dict:
    msg = BytesParser(policy=policy.default).parsebytes(path.read_bytes())
    out = {
        "id": path.stem,
        "headers": {h.replace("-", "_"): msg.get(h) for h in HEADERS},
        "text": None,
        "html": None,
        "attachments": [],
    }
    stack = [msg]
    while stack:
        part = stack.pop(0)
        ct = part.get_content_type()
        if ct == "message/rfc822":
            data = (
                part.get_payload(0).as_bytes()
                if part.is_multipart()
                else part.get_payload(decode=True)
            )
            _add(out, part, data, files, default=f"attached-{len(out['attachments']) + 1}.eml")
            continue
        if part.is_multipart():
            stack[0:0] = list(part.iter_parts())
            continue
        disp = part.get_content_disposition()
        if disp in ("attachment", "inline") and (part.get_filename() or ct.split("/")[0] != "text"):
            _add(out, part, part.get_payload(decode=True) or b"", files)
        elif ct == "text/plain" and out["text"] is None:
            out["text"] = _text(part)
        elif ct == "text/html" and out["html"] is None:
            out["html"] = _text(part)
    return out


def _add(out, part, data: bytes, files: Path | None, default: str = "unnamed") -> None:
    name = part.get_filename() or default
    item = {
        "filename": name,
        "mime": part.get_content_type(),
        "size": len(data),
        "inline": part.get_content_disposition() == "inline",
        "content_id": (part.get("Content-ID") or "").strip("<>") or None,
        "path": None,
    }
    if files:
        p = files / out["id"] / _safe(name)
        p.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        p.write_bytes(data)
        item["path"] = str(p)
    out["attachments"].append(item)


def main(argv=None) -> int:
    sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8")
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__, formatter_class=argparse.RawTextHelpFormatter)

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Optional helper: .eml -> JSON + attachment files.  Use it, port it, or ignore it.  Stdlib only.

    python eml_to_json.py dev/emails/E001.eml                      # one email -> stdout
    python eml_to_json.py dev/emails --out inbox.json --files att  # all emails; attachments saved

Shape: {id, headers{from,to,cc,date,subject,message_id,in_reply_to,references},
        text, html, attachments:[{filename, mime, size, inline, content_id, path}]}
`path` is set only with --files (bytes written to <files>/<id>/<filename>).  A forwarded or
bounced message attached as message/rfc822 is saved as a .eml file.  Reading what is INSIDE an
attachment (Excel, PDF, scans, photos ...) is up to you.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import re
import sys
from email import policy
from email.parser import BytesParser
from pathlib import Path

HEADERS = ("from", "to", "cc", "date", "subject", "message-id", "in-reply-to", "references")


def _text(part) -> str:
    try:
        return part.get_content()
    except Exception:  # unknown charset / bad transfer encoding
        return (part.get_payload(decode=True) or b"").decode("utf-8", "replace")


def _safe(name: str) -> str:
    return re.sub(r"[^\w.\- ]+", "_", name).strip() or "unnamed"


def eml_to_json(path: Path, files: Path | None = None) -> dict:
    msg = BytesParser(policy=policy.default).parsebytes(path.read_bytes())
    out = {
        "id": path.stem,
        "headers": {h.replace("-", "_"): msg.get(h) for h in HEADERS},
        "text": None,
        "html": None,
        "attachments": [],
    }
    stack = [msg]
    while stack:
        part = stack.pop(0)
        ct = part.get_content_type()
        if ct == "message/rfc822":
            data = (
                part.get_payload(0).as_bytes()
                if part.is_multipart()
                else part.get_payload(decode=True)
            )
            _add(out, part, data, files, default=f"attached-{len(out['attachments']) + 1}.eml")
            continue
        if part.is_multipart():
            stack[0:0] = list(part.iter_parts())
            continue
        disp = part.get_content_disposition()
        if disp in ("attachment", "inline") and (part.get_filename() or ct.split("/")[0] != "text"):
            _add(out, part, part.get_payload(decode=True) or b"", files)
        elif ct == "text/plain" and out["text"] is None:
            out["text"] = _text(part)
        elif ct == "text/html" and out["html"] is None:
            out["html"] = _text(part)
    return out


def _add(out, part, data: bytes, files: Path | None, default: str = "unnamed") -> None:
    name = part.get_filename() or default
    item = {
        "filename": name,
        "mime": part.get_content_type(),
        "size": len(data),
        "inline": part.get_content_disposition() == "inline",
        "content_id": (part.get("Content-ID") or "").strip("<>") or None,
        "path": None,
    }
    if files:
        p = files / out["id"] / _safe(name)
        p.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        p.write_bytes(data)
        item["path"] = str(p)
    out["attachments"].append(item)


def main(argv=None) -> int:
    sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8")
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__, formatter_class=argparse.RawTextHelpFormatter)
    ap.add_argument("path", type=Path, help=".eml file or a directory of them")
    ap.add_argument("--out", type=Path, help="write JSON here instead of stdout")
    ap.add_argument("--files", type=Path, help="save attachment bytes under this directory")
    a = ap.parse_args(argv)
    if a.path.is_dir():
        data = {p.stem: eml_to_json(p, a.files) for p in sorted(a.path.glob("*.eml"))}
    else:
        data = eml_to_json(a.path, a.files)
    s = json.dumps(data, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)
    if a.out:
        a.out.write_text(s + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
    else:
        print(s)
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json

        "needs_review": True,

    result = parse_dir(args.emails)
    args.out.write_text(json.dumps(result, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
